## Hope Valley Health Care Association

The Hope Valley Health Care Association owns and operates six nursing homes in adjoining states. 

An evaluation of their efficiency has been undertaken using two inputs and two outputs.

The inputs are staffing labor (measured in average hours per day) and the cost of supplies (in thousands of dollars per day). 

The outputs are the number of patient-days reimbursed by third-party sources and the number of patient-days reimbursed privately. A summary of performance data is shown in the table below.

***

## Load the libraries
Install the Benchmarking library.
```{r}
#install.packages("Benchmarking")
library(Benchmarking)
```
## 1. DEA analysis

## Enter the data
Each row represents one facility. The first input column contains staffing hours, and the second contains supplies cost.

The first output column contains reimbursed patient-days, and the second contains privately paid patient-days.

```{r}
x <- matrix(
  c(
    150, 400, 320, 520, 350, 320,
    0.2, 0.7, 1.2, 2.0, 1.2, 0.7
  ),
  ncol = 2
)

y <- matrix(
  c(
    14000, 14000, 42000, 28000, 19000, 14000,
    3500, 21000, 10500, 42000, 25000, 15000
  ),
  ncol = 2
)

colnames(x) <- c("Staff Hours", "Supplies")
colnames(y) <- c("Reimbursed Patient-Days", "Private Patient-Days")

rownames(x) <- c(
  "Facility 1", "Facility 2", "Facility 3",
  "Facility 4", "Facility 5", "Facility 6"
)

rownames(y) <- rownames(x)

x
y
```
***
## DEA model formulation

This analysis uses input-oriented DEA. For each facility, the model minimizes the proportion of its current staffing and supplies needed to maintain its observed patient-days. The benchmark must produce at least as many patient-days in each output category.

The lambda weights determine which facilities make up the benchmark.
Their restrictions depend on the model:

| Model | Lambda restrictions |
|:------|:--------------------|
| FDH | Each lambda is 0 or 1, and their sum equals 1 |
| CRS | Nonnegative lambdas with no sum restriction |
| VRS | Nonnegative lambdas whose sum equals 1 |
| IRS | Nonnegative lambdas whose sum is at least 1 |
| DRS | Nonnegative lambdas whose sum is at most 1 |
| FRH | Nonnegative integer lambdas with no sum restriction |

A score below 1 indicates that proportional input reductions are possible. A score of 1 indicates that the model found no proportional input reduction.

***
The following sections show each model's efficiency scores, peers, and lambda weights, addressing Questions 1 and 2.

## FDH: Free Disposability Hull

FDH compares facilities against individual observed facilities without assuming convexity.

```{r}
e_fdh <- dea(x, y, RTS = "fdh")
e_fdh

peers(e_fdh)

lambda(e_fdh, KEEPREF = TRUE)
```

***

## CRS: Constant Returns to Scale

CRS allows convex combinations and proportional scaling up or down.

```{r}
e_crs <- dea(x, y, RTS = "crs")
e_crs

peers(e_crs)

lambda(e_crs, KEEPREF = TRUE)
```

***

## VRS: Variable Returns to Scale

VRS allows convex combinations of facilities, with lambdas that
sum to 1.

```{r}
e_vrs <- dea(x, y, RTS = "vrs")
e_vrs

peers(e_vrs)

lambda(e_vrs, KEEPREF = TRUE)
```

***

## IRS: Increasing Returns to Scale

IRS allows convex combinations and scaling up. The lambdas must
sum to at least 1.

```{r}
e_irs <- dea(x, y, RTS = "irs")
e_irs

peers(e_irs)

lambda(e_irs, KEEPREF = TRUE)
```

***

## DRS: Decreasing Returns to Scale

DRS allows convex combinations and scaling down. The lambdas must
sum to at most 1.

```{r}
e_drs <- dea(x, y, RTS = "drs")
e_drs

peers(e_drs)

lambda(e_drs, KEEPREF = TRUE)
```

***

## FRH: Free Replicability Hull

FRH allows addition and whole-number replication of observed
production plans. In Benchmarking, this model uses RTS = "add".

```{r}
e_frh <- dea(x, y, RTS = "add")
e_frh

peers(e_frh)

lambda(e_frh, KEEPREF = TRUE)
```

***

## 3. Results summary

The following table compares the efficiency scores under all six
assumptions.

```{r}
efficiency_summary <- data.frame(
  Facility = rownames(x),
  FDH = eff(e_fdh),
  CRS = eff(e_crs),
  VRS = eff(e_vrs),
  IRS = eff(e_irs),
  DRS = eff(e_drs),
  FRH = eff(e_frh)
)

knitr::kable(
  efficiency_summary,
  digits = 6,
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

***

## 4. Compare and contrast the results

Facilities 1 through 4 have an efficiency score of 1 under all six models. Facilities 5 and 6 have different results depending on the assumptions used.

Under FDH and FRH, all six facilities have a score of 1. Under VRS and IRS, Facility 5 still has a score of 1, while Facility 6 has a score of approximately 0.8963.

CRS and DRS give the lowest scores. Facility 5 has a score of approximately 0.9775, and Facility 6 has a score of approximately 0.8675. Facility 6 therefore has the greatest potential for proportional input reduction.

The peer groups also change. Under CRS and DRS, Facilities 5 and 6 both use Facilities 1, 2, and 4 as peers. Under VRS and IRS, Facility 6 uses Facilities 1, 2, and 5.

For this dataset, CRS and DRS produce the same results, as do VRS and IRS. The comparison shows that allowing different combinations and scaling of facilities can change the efficiency scores.
